passage:
Dear Imran,

Thank you for not laughing when I told you on Sunday. I had been checking my crush's profile every few minutes: during physics, at dinner, at midnight. Last week's test came back with silly mistakes, and I didn't want to admit that a person I barely talk to was taking over my whole head. So I have logged out of the app on my phone and I look once at night, briefly. I also started the model for the science exhibition. The glue and cardboard fill the space that all the thinking used to. It hasn't gone away, but it is quieter. Could you ask me on Friday how it's going?

Kavitha

qa.q: What had Kavitha been checking every few minutes?
qa.a: Kavitha had been checking a crush's profile every few minutes.

qa.q: What worried Kavitha about the thoughts, and what showed it?
qa.a: Kavitha was worried and a little embarrassed that the thoughts were crowding out study, shown by the silly mistakes on last week's test.

qa.q: What else could Kavitha do if the thoughts stay strong, and why?
qa.a: Kavitha could talk to a parent or the school counsellor as well, because more support helps when a worry keeps taking over.

qa.q: How might Imran feel on reading the letter?
qa.a: Imran likely feels trusted and glad to help, especially with a request to ask again on Friday.

grounding: Noticing that thoughts about the crush crowd out study, the student limits checking online, tells a trusted person, and puts the energy into a project, which lowers the intensity.
